title: Abolition of Capitalism
summary: DSA's constitution calls outright for "the abolition of capitalism." Historically, every large-scale attempt to eliminate market economies produced severe shortages and required increasing coercion to maintain. US impact: the world's largest economy would be restructured around central planning, with predictable effects on investment, employment, and consumer goods availability.
history: Every 20th-century attempt to abolish capitalism at national scale — the Soviet Union, Maoist China, Cuba, and later Venezuela — followed a similar arc: initial nationalization of major industries, followed by production shortfalls as price signals and profit incentives disappeared, followed by rationing, black markets, and expanded state control to manage the resulting scarcity. None of these transitions were peaceful or voluntary at the point where private ownership was actually seized.
debunked: DSA and its defenders often argue that prior failures reflect authoritarian implementation rather than the economic model itself, and that a democratic, gradual transition would avoid these outcomes. But the shortages in these historical cases were not primarily caused by political repression — they followed directly from removing price signals and profit incentives that coordinate production and distribution in a market economy. Gradualism does not solve this: partial abolition (as in Venezuela's price controls and expropriations) produced the same shortage dynamics on a smaller scale before authoritarian measures were even introduced.
usImpact: The US economy is the largest and most complex in the world, coordinating millions of independent pricing and production decisions daily. Abolishing capitalism at that scale would require replacing this coordination mechanism with centralized planning — a system no government has operated successfully at US scale. The likely near-term effects: capital flight, collapse in business investment, and disruption to supply chains that currently depend on decentralized price signals to allocate resources efficiently.

title: Abolishing the Senate
summary: DSA Co-Chair Megan Romer confirmed on Fox News that DSA supports abolishing the Senate, replacing the presidency and Supreme Court with a body "subordinate to Congress." This mirrors a common revolutionary-government structure: concentrating power in a single legislative body with no independent checks.
history: Concentrating executive, legislative, and judicial power into a single body subordinate to one chamber has a well-documented history, most notably in early revolutionary France's National Convention (1792–1795), which combined legislative and executive functions and presided over the Reign of Terror, and in Soviet-model systems where the Supreme Soviet nominally held ultimate authority over a judiciary with no independent power of review.
debunked: Proponents argue the Senate is undemocratic due to unequal state representation and that reform, not danger, is the goal. That critique of the Senate's structure is a legitimate policy debate. But DSA's stated position goes further than reform — it calls for eliminating the separation of powers itself, not adjusting how the Senate is composed. Removing judicial and executive independence removes the primary mechanism by which US law constrains legislative majorities, regardless of who holds that majority.
usImpact: The separation of powers is the core structural safeguard against a single political faction controlling government outright. Eliminating the Senate and subordinating the presidency and courts to Congress would remove the checks that require broad coalition-building to pass and enforce law, concentrating power in whichever party controls the House at a given moment — a structure with no precedent for peaceful transfer of power out of the party that removed these checks.

title: Replacing the Presidency and Supreme Court
summary: DSA's platform calls for replacing the presidency and Supreme Court with "an executive and judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress." This eliminates judicial review and independent executive authority in favor of legislative supremacy.
history: Legislative supremacy models — where courts and executives serve at the pleasure of the legislature rather than as independent branches — have historically enabled rapid, unchecked policy shifts. The Soviet judiciary, formally subordinate to the Communist Party-controlled state apparatus, could not rule against the government on constitutional grounds because no independent constitutional authority existed above the legislature.
debunked: Supporters frame this as democratizing the judiciary, arguing that unelected judges wielding lifetime appointments are themselves undemocratic. That critique has some basis — judicial appointments are indeed insulated from voters. But subordinating courts to Congress does not make courts more democratic; it removes their ability to check Congress at all, including when Congress violates individual rights that a simple legislative majority opposes.
usImpact: Judicial review is the mechanism by which the Bill of Rights is enforced against legislative majorities. A judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress could not meaningfully rule against a sitting Congress on constitutional grounds, removing the primary check against majoritarian overreach on speech, religion, due process, and other constitutional protections.

title: Abolishing ICE and Open Borders
summary: DSA's platform calls for abolishing ICE and existing border enforcement. Historically, countries that dramatically loosened border and immigration enforcement without capacity planning experienced strain on housing, labor markets, and public services.
history: Large, unplanned migration surges — such as Europe's 2015 migration crisis — demonstrated that enforcement capacity and integration infrastructure (housing, language services, labor market absorption) matter as much as border policy itself. Countries that scaled back enforcement without corresponding investment in integration systems saw significant strain on municipal services and public support for migration policy erode rapidly.
debunked: Advocates argue ICE's tactics (family separation, workplace raids) are disproportionate to its stated mission and that enforcement can be replaced by other means. Reforming or restructuring enforcement is a legitimate policy position. But "abolish" as stated in DSA's platform is a specific position — the elimination of the federal immigration enforcement agency itself, not a reform of its practices, which is a materially different policy with different consequences for who enforces immigration law and how.
usImpact: Eliminating the primary federal immigration enforcement agency without a replacement structure would functionally end interior immigration enforcement. Combined with open border language, this would remove the primary mechanisms controlling both entry and post-entry enforcement, with direct effects on labor market wage pressure in low-skill sectors, strain on local social services in high-migration areas, and law enforcement's ability to coordinate on cross-border criminal activity.

title: Abolishing Prisons
summary: DSA-aligned figures, including Texas legislator James Talarico, have publicly argued prisons should be dismantled, framing incarceration itself as violence. Historical attempts to sharply reduce incarceration without replacement systems have produced measurable increases in recidivism and victimization.
history: Deinstitutionalization efforts in other contexts — most notably the mass closure of psychiatric institutions in the US in the 1960s–80s without adequate community mental health infrastructure — offer a cautionary parallel: removing an institution without building the replacement capacity first shifted the burden onto communities and the criminal justice system, worsening outcomes for the very population the reform intended to help.
debunked: Prison abolitionists argue the current system disproportionately harms marginalized communities and that alternatives like restorative justice can replace incarceration. Sentencing reform and addressing disparities are legitimate, evidence-supported policy goals. But full abolition without a functioning replacement system for violent and repeat offenders is a different claim — no US jurisdiction has successfully eliminated incarceration for serious violent crime while maintaining public safety outcomes at scale.
usImpact: Removing incarceration as a consequence for serious crime, without a demonstrated at-scale alternative, would remove the primary mechanism by which violent and repeat offenders are separated from the public. Historical partial experiments with reduced enforcement and shortened sentencing in specific US cities have correlated with measurable increases in repeat offending among the highest-risk population.

title: Defunding the Pentagon
summary: DSA's platform calls for defunding the Pentagon. Historically, sharp, rapid reductions in military spending without a phased drawdown have degraded readiness and left capability gaps that took years or decades to rebuild.
history: The post-Cold War "peace dividend" drawdown of the 1990s, though far more gradual than DSA's proposal, still produced readiness gaps that defense analysts flagged well into the 2000s. More abrupt drawdowns, such as the post-WWII demobilization, left the US underprepared for the Korean War just five years later.
debunked: Supporters argue defense spending is bloated and that redirected funds could address domestic priorities. Waste and inefficiency in defense procurement is a well-documented, bipartisan concern. But "defunding" as a platform position is a different claim from procurement reform — it targets the overall budget rather than specific inefficiencies, with consequences for force readiness independent of whether the underlying spending was efficiently allocated.
usImpact: The US military underpins alliance commitments (NATO, Indo-Pacific partnerships) and deterrence relationships that a sudden funding cut would directly weaken, with downstream effects on allied confidence and adversary calculus that are difficult to reverse quickly once readiness gaps open.

title: Government Ownership of Large Corporations
summary: DSA Co-Chair Megan Romer confirmed the platform includes government ownership of large corporations. State ownership of major industry has a long, largely negative track record on efficiency, innovation, and consumer outcomes compared to competitive private markets.
history: State-owned enterprises in sectors from airlines to telecommunications — across dozens of 20th-century examples, from British Leyland to Soviet-era manufacturing combines — consistently underperformed private-sector competitors on cost efficiency, product quality, and innovation once compared head-to-head after later privatization.
debunked: Advocates point to specific successful state enterprises (e.g., some national utilities or transit systems) as counterexamples. Isolated successful cases exist, generally in natural-monopoly sectors with limited competitive pressure to begin with (utilities, rail). But DSA's platform targets "large corporations" broadly, including firms in competitive markets like technology and consumer goods, where the historical record of state ownership replacing competitive private ownership is overwhelmingly negative.
usImpact: Extending state ownership to large US corporations across competitive sectors would remove the competitive pressure that currently drives innovation and cost efficiency in industries like technology, retail, and manufacturing, with the state assuming operational and financial risk currently borne by shareholders and subject to market discipline.

title: Decommodifying Housing
summary: DSA's housing platform calls for "decommodifying" housing — treating rent control not as a standalone policy but as a step toward removing housing from private markets entirely. Rent control has a long empirical record of reducing housing supply over time.
history: Rent control has been studied extensively, including in New York City and San Francisco, where economists across the political spectrum have documented reduced construction of new rental units, landlord disinvestment in existing controlled units, and reduced housing mobility as tenants stay in below-market units longer than they otherwise would.
debunked: Supporters argue rent control protects existing tenants from displacement, which is true in the short term for those tenants. But DSA's own framing describes rent control as a "non-reformist reform" — an intentional first step toward full decommodification, not a standalone tenant-protection measure — meaning the stated goal extends well beyond the immediate protective effect proponents cite.
usImpact: Applied at city or national scale, decommodification would reduce private investment in new housing construction precisely when the US faces a well-documented housing supply shortage, worsening the affordability crisis the policy is intended to solve by removing the primary incentive (profit) that currently drives private housing construction.

title: Municipal Grocery Stores
summary: NYC Mayor Mamdani, a documented DSA member, opened five city-run grocery stores with prices set 30% below retail. Economists across the spectrum have noted this mirrors DSA's "decommodification" strategy applied to a specific market.
history: Subsidized state competition against private retailers has been tried in various forms — from Soviet state grocery stores to Venezuela's subsidized food distribution networks (Mercal/PDVAL) — and in each case produced private retailer closures in the subsidized sector, followed by supply shortages once state distribution networks proved unable to match the logistics and incentive structures of private retail at scale.
debunked: Supporters argue the stores address a genuine affordability crisis and that subsidized competition benefits consumers. Genuine affordability challenges are real. But the mechanism — government stores subsidized by tax revenue undercutting private retailers on price — creates a structural disadvantage for private grocers, who cannot compete with subsidized pricing, risking exactly the kind of supply concentration into fewer state-run outlets seen in prior examples.
usImpact: If private grocers exit markets they can no longer compete in, the city becomes more dependent on state-run distribution for food access — concentrating risk in a system with far less logistics experience and no profit-driven incentive to maintain product diversity, freshness, or supply chain reliability compared to established private grocery chains.

title: Wealth Taxes and Public Property Owner Lists
summary: Mamdani's administration published names and addresses of NYC property owners subject to a new "pied-à-terre" tax. Critics, including the NY Post, noted this public list creates targeting risk independent of the tax policy's merits.
history: Publicly naming individuals by wealth or property ownership for political or tax purposes has historical precedent in various "enemies list" and public-shaming campaigns, and has, in documented cases, preceded harassment or targeted violence against the named individuals, regardless of the publishing government's original intent.
debunked: Proponents argue publicity increases tax compliance transparency and that property ownership records are already public in most jurisdictions. Property records being technically public and a government actively compiling and publishing a targeted list for political messaging are different acts — the latter concentrates and publicizes information in a way that increases visibility and targeting risk beyond routine record availability.
usImpact: Regardless of the tax policy's fiscal merits, publicly naming individuals as targets for wealth redistribution creates a documented category of risk — harassment, threats, or violence directed at named individuals — that is a foreseeable consequence independent of whether the underlying tax itself is sound policy.

title: Private Property Abolition
summary: DSA's platform includes language calling for abolishing private property, extending beyond housing and large corporations to a broader property rights framework. This has the deepest and most consistently negative historical record of any DSA platform position.
history: Abolition of private property was the defining structural feature of every major 20th-century communist state — the USSR, Maoist China, and Khmer Rouge Cambodia among them — and in each case was accompanied by mass economic disruption during the transition period, as functioning ownership and incentive structures were dismantled faster than replacement systems could be built.
debunked: Some DSA-aligned voices argue the platform language targets only large-scale capital (factories, land holdings) rather than personal possessions. That distinction, if genuinely limited to productive capital, is narrower than full abolition and worth noting. But DSA's own platform language does not consistently draw this line, and "abolition of private property" as stated is the same phrase used historically to describe full-scale seizure, not a targeted capital-ownership reform.
usImpact: Even a narrowly targeted version — abolishing private ownership of productive capital (factories, land, business assets) — would eliminate the ownership stake that currently incentivizes investment, maintenance, and long-term planning by owners, a dynamic with no successful large-scale substitute demonstrated anywhere at US economic scale.

title: Police Abolition and Defunding
summary: DSA-aligned figures have called for defunding and abolishing police departments, paired with the broader prison abolition platform. Cities that implemented significant police budget cuts in the early 2020s saw measurable increases in violent crime rates before most reversed course.
history: Several major US cities reduced police budgets and staffing significantly in 2020–2021. In the years that followed, most of these same cities reported rising violent crime and, in several cases, reversed the funding cuts and rebuilt police staffing levels after the initial reductions correlated with worsening public safety outcomes.
debunked: Advocates argue that redirecting police funding toward social services addresses root causes of crime more effectively than policing. Investment in social services and crime-prevention infrastructure is a reasonable complement to public safety policy. But the empirical record from the specific US cities that tested reduced police funding as a standalone measure — without simultaneously building out replacement crisis-response infrastructure at matching scale — showed a correlation with worse, not better, public safety outcomes in the short-to-medium term.
usImpact: Reducing police staffing and funding without first building out at-scale alternative crisis response infrastructure risks repeating the pattern seen in cities that tried this in 2020–2021: reduced response capacity, longer emergency response times, and measurable increases in reported violent crime before any policy reversal could take effect.
